paraphrase: Ānanda, a wealthy householder of Vāṇijagrāma, takes before Mahāvīra the five small vows and seven supplementary vows, limiting his wealth, fields, cattle and trade; later he performs the eleven lay stages (pratimā), gains clairvoyance and dies a peaceful death. When Gautama doubted him, Mahāvīra told Gautama that he, not the layman, must ask forgiveness.

A god appears to the Jain layman Kuṇḍakoliya and praises the teaching of Gosāla Maṅkhaliputta — that there is no exertion, action, strength, energy or human effort, and all things are fixed (niyayā savvabhāvā) — over Mahāvīra's. Kuṇḍakoliya asks how the god gained his divine state: by exertion or without? If without, why are all beings not gods? The god falls silent; Mahāvīra praises the layman.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Uvāsagadasāo (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory.

paraphrase: Saddālaputra, a potter and follower of Gośāla, believed that all happens by fate without effort. Mahāvīra asked him: if a man stole or smashed your pots or assaulted your wife, would you punish him? He said yes — then, said Mahāvīra, you do not really hold that there is no effort or exertion. Saddālaputra became Mahāvīra's lay disciple.
speaker: Mahāvīra
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Uvāsagadasāo (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory.

paraphrase: Gosāla comes to win Saddālaputta back and praises Mahāvīra as the great brāhmaṇa, great cowherd, great guide, great preacher and great pilot; Saddālaputta gives him lodging but not as a teacher, and Gosāla cannot shake him.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Uvāsagadasāo (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory.
